claims.text: Aging a low-density refractory high-entropy alloy at approximately 850 °C for 3 hours will form coherent nanoscale precipitates or ordered domains.
The precipitates produced by this aging treatment will improve elevated-temperature yield strength and creep resistance.
The aging treatment will not significantly increase alloy density.
The aging treatment will preserve room-temperature ductility.
The initial alloy is a homogeneous, as-cast, single-phase refractory high-entropy alloy based on elements such as Nb, Mo, Cr, Ti, and Al.
Existing solute elements in the alloy can be precipitated in situ by a single-step intermediate-temperature aging treatment.
The treatment-induced benefit will persist during service at 800–1100 °C under sustained or cyclic mechanical loading.
Coherent nanoscale precipitates impede dislocation motion at elevated temperatures.
Impeded dislocation motion increases elevated-temperature yield strength and creep resistance.
Precipitate coherency minimizes stress concentrations and thereby preserves room-temperature ductility.
Using only elements already present in the alloy prevents an appreciable change in overall alloy density.
Relative to the untreated as-cast alloy, the aged alloy will have measurably higher high-temperature strength.
Relative to the untreated as-cast alloy, the aged alloy will retain comparable room-temperature ductility and unchanged density.
Aging at excessive temperature can over-coarsen precipitates and reduce strengthening.
Aging at insufficient temperature can produce too little precipitation to provide a significant improvement.
The proposed benefit is limited to refractory alloys capable of forming coherent precipitates without forming brittle phases.
